newsitem.title: IRAQ: U.N. experts to oversee Iraqis dig for missiles.
newsitem.headline: U.N. experts to oversee Iraqis dig for missiles.

text.p: Iraq will soon start new excavations at its missile sites to provide evidence that it has destroyed all its long-range missiles banned under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms, a senior U.N. arms official said on Sunday.

Goran Wallen, head of Baghdad's Ongoing Monitoring and Verfication Centre (OMV), said a team of U.N. missile experts was due in Baghdad on Monday to supervise Iraqi digs expected to take place at sites close to Baghdad.
"It is very clear that Iraq has not accounted for a number of missiles. Iraq must carry out more excavations to prove that the missiles in question are really destroyed," he told Reuters.

Wallen said the current row was over the number of missile engines Iraq had imported from the former Soviet Union. He said the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) overseeing the destruction of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction still needed evidence that all such engines were scrapped.
A senior Iraqi official was quoted on Sunday as saying that Iraq was gathering evidence to counter U.N. statements about the existence of banned missiles in its arsenal.

General Amer Hammoudi al-Saadi, an adviser at the presidential office, did not say in the newspaper remarks whether Iraq would heed a U.N. demand to have missile parts analysed by international experts in the United States.
UNSCOM has most of the parts packed in boxes ready for shipment abroad. The rest are stored in warehouses in Baghdad under strict U.N. surveillance.
Wallen said UNSCOM would only drop its demand to take the parts outside if the forthcoming digs unearth "conclusive evidence that the engines in question were definitely scrapped".
The U.N. Security Council censured Iraq on December 30 for refusing to allow more than 100 missile engines to be taken abroad for examination by experts.

Saadi said Iraq had a clear idea of UNSCOM's claims and "this would help us work in a scientific and documented manner to refute them by supplying the international community with convincing material evidence proving that Iraq is telling the truth," the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya reported.
"General Saadi...confirmed that Iraq is continuing with its full and objective cooperation with UNSCOM and the long-term (arms) monitoring centre in Baghdad," it said.
"Everybody knows that Iraq is telling the truth and we do not hide anything and UNSCOM could not condemn Iraq in a direct form or in a scientific and documented manner," Saadi told the newspaper.

UNSCOM chairman Rolf Ekeus reported during his December visit to Baghdad that he believed Iraq still had "a significant number of operational missiles which could constitute a complete missile force".
Ekeus's ballistic missile experts say they still lack a full accounting of rockets with a range greater than 150 km (95 miles) which Baghdad is banned from possessing or manufacturing.
Ekeus is due in Baghdad in February for another bid to persuade Iraqi leaders to allow the parts be taken abroad.
